pages.textMedium:
Teddy was a bear. A big, tough forest bear. (Do not call him cute. He hates that.)

He had eaten honey for breakfast. He had eaten blueberries for lunch. His paws were sticky and his tongue was blue.

"Enough," said Teddy. "Today I want FISH."
pages.textLong:
Teddy was a bear. A big, tough forest bear. (Do not call him cute. He hates that.)

He had eaten honey for breakfast. He had eaten blueberries for lunch. His paws were sticky and his tongue was blue.

"Enough," said Teddy. "Today I want FISH."

So Teddy stomped off through the forest. STOMP. STOMP. STOMP.

A small bird flew along beside him. "Where are you going?"

"Fishing," said Teddy.

"Have you ever caught a fish?"

"No," said Teddy. "But I have seen one. How hard can it be?"

The bird decided to come and watch.
pages.scene: Teddy marching down a sunny forest path, chest out, chin up, sticky paws swinging. The small bird (the same one as on the later pages) flies beside his ear with a doubtful look. The river glints between the birch trees ahead. Lively detail: a line of ants following his sticky honey paw prints.

pages.textMedium:
So Teddy stomped down to the river. And the river was packed with fish! Silver ones, spotty ones, fat ones, fast ones. They shot past his toes like little rockets.

"Easy," said Teddy, and licked his lips.

It was not easy.
pages.textLong:
And there was the river. And the river was packed with fish! Silver ones, spotty ones, fat ones, fast ones. They shot past his toes like little rockets.

"Easy," said Teddy, and licked his lips.

It was not easy.

pages.textMedium:
He grabbed with his left paw. SPLASH! Nothing. He grabbed with his right paw. SPLASH! Nothing.

He jumped in with all four paws at once. SPLOOSH! He got a wet nose, a wet bottom, and one old stick.
pages.textLong:
He grabbed with his left paw. SPLASH! Nothing. He grabbed with his right paw. SPLASH! Nothing.

He jumped in with all four paws at once. SPLOOSH! He got a wet nose, a wet bottom, and one old stick.

pages.textMedium:
New plan. Teddy stood in the river as still as a rock. He did not blink. He did not breathe. Rocks are very patient.

The fish swam closer. And closer. Then one of them nibbled his toe.

"Hee-hee-HEE!" squealed the rock, and fell over backwards. SPLASH!

"That's four tries," said a small bird on a branch. "I'm counting."
pages.textLong:
New plan. Teddy stood in the river as still as a rock. He did not blink. He did not breathe. Rocks are very patient.

The fish swam closer. And closer. Then one of them nibbled his toe.

"Hee-hee-HEE!" squealed the rock, and fell over backwards. SPLASH!

"That's four tries," said the bird. "I'm counting."
pages.scene: Teddy standing in the river stiff as a statue, arms pressed to his sides, eyes wide and unblinking, cheeks puffed from holding his breath. Under the water a small fish nibbles his big toe while others circle, curious. The small bird watches from a birch branch, head tilted. Lively detail: a frog sits on Teddy's head as if he really were a rock.

pages.textLong:
Next plan. Fish like worms, don't they? Teddy did not have a worm. But he did have a tongue, and it was still blue from lunch.

He lay on the bank and dangled it in the water. Wiggle, wiggle.

The fish came to look at the blue worm. A little one bit it.

"OWTH!" said Teddy.

"Five," said the bird.
pages.scene: Teddy lying on his belly on the grassy bank, chin over the edge, his long blue tongue dangling in the water like a worm. Fish gather round to inspect it, and one tiny fish is just about to bite the tip. Lively detail: the small bird on the bank covers its eyes with one wing but peeks through the feathers.

pages.textMedium:
Then Teddy found a hollow log. Aha! A fish trap! He held it in the river, and a fat silver fish swam straight in.

"GOT YOU!" roared Teddy.

The fish swam straight out the other end. It turned around and did it again, just for fun. Then it fetched its friends.

"Five," said the bird.
pages.textLong:
Then Teddy found a hollow log. Aha! A fish trap! He held it in the river, and a fat silver fish swam straight in.

"GOT YOU!" roared Teddy.

The fish swam straight out the other end. It turned around and did it again, just for fun. Then it fetched its friends.

"Six," said the bird.
pages.scene: Teddy knee-deep in the river holding a hollow log in the current, peering into one end with a triumphant grin. Behind his back a fat silver fish shoots out of the other end, winking. Lively detail: a neat queue of fish waiting their turn at the log's entrance. The small bird watches from its branch.

pages.textLong:
So Teddy climbed a birch tree that leaned out over the water. He would drop on the fish from above, like an eagle. A big, furry eagle.

The birch bent. It bent some more. It lowered him gently into the river, bottom first, and sprang back up.

He caught a mouthful of river weed.

"Seven," said the bird.
pages.scene: A thin birch bent in a great arc over the river with Teddy clinging to the top, his bottom just dipping into the water, face very surprised. Fish look up from below, delighted. Lively detail: the small bird sits calmly on the bent trunk as if it were a slide.

pages.textMedium:
By now the fish were laughing out loud. Blub-blub-blub. One cheeky fish swam right up, slapped him on the nose with its tail, and zipped away.

Teddy tried a hundred times. (The bird counted.) Do you know how many fish he caught? Zero. A big, fat zero.
pages.textLong:
By now the fish were laughing out loud. Blub-blub-blub. One cheeky fish swam right up, slapped him on the nose with its tail, and zipped away.

Teddy tried a hundred times. (The bird counted.) Do you know how many fish he caught? Zero. A big, fat zero.

pages.textMedium:
And the fish? They were having the best day of their lives.

They swam backwards past his knees. They jumped over his head, one after another, like a circus. The cheeky spotted one blew a bubble right in his ear. Pop!

Teddy grabbed left. He grabbed right. He grabbed his own foot by mistake and went under. Glub.
pages.textLong:
And the fish? They were having the best day of their lives.

They swam backwards past his knees. They jumped over his head, one after another, like a circus. The cheeky spotted one blew a bubble right in his ear. Pop!

Teddy grabbed left. He grabbed right. He grabbed his own foot by mistake and went under. Glub.
pages.scene: Teddy standing in the river grabbing at the air with both paws, wobbling on one leg, while fish leap in a high arc over his head one after another like circus performers. The cheeky spotted fish (from the nose-slap page) blows a bubble beside his ear. Lively detail: one fish swims past his knees backwards, waving a fin.

pages.textMedium:
Teddy climbed out and sat down on a rock. His belly growled. His lip wobbled. And then — don't tell anyone — big, fat tears rolled down his furry cheeks.

"I'm the worst fisher-bear in the whole forest," he sniffed.

The bird stopped counting.
pages.textLong:
Teddy climbed out and sat down on a rock. His belly growled. His lip wobbled. And then — don't tell anyone — big, fat tears rolled down his furry cheeks.

"I'm the worst fisher-bear in the whole forest," he sniffed.

The bird stopped counting.

He could go home. There was more honey at home. There were more blueberries.

Teddy looked at his sticky paws. He looked at his blue tongue. (Go on, try to look at your own tongue. It's hard.)

Honey for breakfast. Blueberries for lunch. And for dinner?

His belly growled one word: FISH.
pages.scene: Teddy still on the rock, tears drying, going cross-eyed as he tries to look at his own stuck-out blue tongue, sticky paws held up in front of him. A thought cloud shows a honey pot and a blueberry bush, and he pulls a face at it. Lively detail: the small bird on its branch is trying to look at its own tongue too.

pages.textMedium:
He wiped his nose with his paw. His sticky, honey paw. (That's going to matter in a minute.)

Then he took a big breath. "One more time," said Teddy. "A bear doesn't quit." And he stood up tall.

"A hundred and one!" cheered the bird.
pages.textLong:
He wiped his nose with his paw. His sticky, honey paw. (That's going to matter in a minute.)

Then he took a big breath. "One more time," said Teddy. "A bear doesn't quit." And he stood up tall.

"A hundred and one!" cheered the bird.

Teddy waded back into the river. Slowly. He planted his feet. He lifted both paws. He made his meanest fishing face.

The fish lined up to watch. This was going to be good.

The cheeky spotted one swam right up to his nose and wiggled its tail at him. That tail.

Teddy was just about to grab it, when...
pages.scene: Teddy in the river with feet planted wide, both paws raised, his fiercest fishing face, nose shiny with honey. The fish are lined up in a tidy row like an audience. The cheeky spotted fish hangs right in front of his nose, wiggling its tail. Lively detail: on the bank the dandelion clocks are just starting to sway in a breeze.

pages.textMedium:
Just then, a breeze shook the dandelions on the riverbank. A hundred fluffy seeds floated up into the air — and three of them landed right on his sticky, honey nose.

Tickle. Tickle. Tickle.
pages.textLong:
Just then, a breeze shook the dandelions on the riverbank. A hundred fluffy seeds floated up into the air — and three of them landed right on his sticky, honey nose.

Tickle. Tickle. Tickle.

pages.textMedium:
Oh no. Not now.

Teddy wrinkled his nose. He held his breath. He pressed a paw under his nose — the sticky paw, which did not help at all.

"Ah..." Nothing. Phew.

"Ah... ah..." Nothing. Phew.

The fish stopped laughing. The bird held on to its branch with both feet. Would you have stayed to watch?
pages.textLong:
Oh no. Not now.

Teddy wrinkled his nose. He held his breath. He pressed a paw under his nose — the sticky paw, which did not help at all.

"Ah..." Nothing. Phew.

"Ah... ah..." Nothing. Phew.

The fish stopped laughing. The bird held on to its branch with both feet. Would you have stayed to watch?
pages.scene: Teddy with his head tipped back, one sticky paw pressed under his nose, eyes watering, cheeks puffed, three dandelion seeds on his honey-shiny nose. In the water the fish back away nervously. Lively detail: the small bird grips its branch with both feet, feathers ruffled, eyes squeezed shut.

pages.textMedium:
"Ah... ah... AH-CHOOOO!"

It was the biggest sneeze the forest had ever heard. Birds fell off their branches. The sneeze hit the river like a cannonball, and the water spun round and round and up, up, UP!
pages.textLong:
"Ah... ah... AH-CHOOOO!"

It was the biggest sneeze the forest had ever heard. Birds fell off their branches. The sneeze hit the river like a cannonball, and the water spun round and round and up, up, UP!

And the sneeze kept going. It blew the fluff off every dandelion. It blew a squirrel's tail inside out like an umbrella. It rolled right across the forest and blew the blanket off grumpy old Grandpa Bear, who was having a nap.

"WHO SNEEZED?" roared Grandpa Bear.

Nobody answered. Everybody was looking up. Because above the river...
pages.scene: Deeper in the forest, a new place: Grandpa Bear's nap spot under a big tree. Grey, grumpy Grandpa Bear (the one from the feast page) sits bolt upright as his blanket flies away on a gust full of dandelion fluff and leaves. On a branch a squirrel (the squirrel from the Ice Fishing story) clings on, its tail blown inside out like an umbrella. Lively detail: far behind them a spiral of water is rising above the treetops, and everyone is staring at it.

pages.textMedium:
A FISH TORNADO! Silver ones, spotty ones, fat ones, fast ones — all whirling through the air. And then they came down.

Flop, flop, flop, flop, all around Teddy, like shiny rain. One landed right on his head, like a hat.

Who's laughing now, fish?
pages.textLong:
A FISH TORNADO! Silver ones, spotty ones, fat ones, fast ones — all whirling through the air. And then they came down.

Flop, flop, flop, flop, all around Teddy, like shiny rain. One landed right on his head, like a hat.

Who's laughing now, fish?

pages.textMedium:
When the tornado was finished, the river was quiet and the bank was not.

There were fish in the grass. Fish in the dandelions. Fish up the birch trees. There was even a fish in the bird's nest.

The bird began to count. It gave up.

"Lots," said the bird. "And one old stick."
pages.textLong:
When the tornado was finished, the river was quiet and the bank was not.

There were fish in the grass. Fish in the dandelions. Fish up the birch trees. There was even a fish in the bird's nest.

The bird began to count. It gave up.

"Lots," said the bird. "And one old stick."
pages.scene: The riverbank after the tornado: fish lying in the grass, among the dandelions and hanging in the birch branches, the river calm again. Teddy stands in the middle, amazed, a fish still on his head like a hat. The small bird stands beside its nest with a fish sitting in it, wing on hip, not pleased. Lively detail: the old stick from the belly-flop page lies on top of the fish pile.

pages.textMedium:
It was far too many fish for one bear. Even a hungry one. So Teddy invited every bear in the forest.

They came at sunset. Big bears. Small bears. And last of all, grumpy old Grandpa Bear, with dandelion fluff in his ears.

"Was that sneeze YOU?" he growled.

"Yes," said Teddy. "Fish?"

Grandpa Bear thought about it. "Fish," he said.
pages.textLong:
It was far too many fish for one bear. Even a hungry one. So Teddy invited every bear in the forest.

They came at sunset. Big bears. Small bears. And last of all, grumpy old Grandpa Bear, with dandelion fluff in his ears.

"Was that sneeze YOU?" he growled.

"Yes," said Teddy. "Fish?"

Grandpa Bear thought about it. "Fish," he said.
pages.scene: Sunset on the riverbank. Teddy stands proudly beside a huge pile of fish and a freshly lit campfire, holding one fish out. Bears of all sizes arrive along the path; last comes grey Grandpa Bear, frowning, with dandelion fluff stuck in his ears. The small bird sits on Teddy's shoulder. Lively detail: a tiny bear cub is already dragging away a fish as big as itself.

pages.textMedium:
That night they ate fish until their bellies were as round as the moon. Nobody asked for honey. Nobody asked for blueberries.

Then they lay down by the fire in one big heap. Teddy fell asleep with a smile on his face and a fishbone for a toothpick. Because even the toughest bear in the forest has to sleep sometime.
